questions.question: Regarding long-term outcomes and prognosis in mechanically ventilated COPD patients:
questions.explanation: Pre-morbid functional status, nutritional state, comorbidities, and prior exacerbation history all influence long-term prognosis after MV for AECOPD — factors that clinicians should consider before deciding on ventilatory support. Six-month mortality ranges from 40–70% across studies (not 5–15%), substantially worse than most other ICU respiratory failure aetiologies. In contrast, acute asthma requiring MV does not per se worsen long-term asthma prognosis — the long-term outlook in asthma depends on longitudinal lung function changes from airway inflammation, not on the acute episode. Five-year survival after MV for AECOPD may approach 10% (mortality ~90%) — not 80–90% survival.
questions.section: Part V: Supportive Therapies and Complications

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reported 6-month mortality rate for mechanically ventilated COPD ranges from 5–15%, similar to outcomes following ICU admission for community-acquired pneumonia

statements.label: B
statements.text: The majority of patients with severe acute asthma who require invasive mechanical ventilation have a favourable long-term lung function prognosis, as MV itself does not worsen long-term asthma outcomes

statements.label: C
statements.text: Five-year survival rates following MV for AECOPD approach 80–90% when cardiovascular comorbidities are aggressively managed with evidence-based therapies

statements.label: D
statements.text: Long-term prognosis for mechanically ventilated COPD patients is influenced by pre-morbid functional status, nutritional state, and comorbidities

questions.question: Intrinsic PEEP (PEEPi) is:
questions.explanation: Intrinsic PEEP (auto-PEEP, PEEPi) is the positive alveolar pressure that persists at end-expiration due to incomplete lung emptying, and represents the lowest average alveolar pressure reached during the respiratory cycle. It is measured with an end-expiratory hold manoeuvre (occlusion of the expiratory port just before the next inspiration), reading the plateau pressure that develops - not by subtracting set PEEP from Pplat, which reflects total respiratory system compliance instead. Unlike set (extrinsic) PEEP, PEEPi has no fixed normal range; in health it is close to zero, while in obstructive lung disease with dynamic hyperinflation it can be substantially elevated.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Measured by subtraction of set PEEP from the plateau (Pplat) pressure

statements.label: B
statements.text: The lowest average alveolar pressure during the respiratory cycle

statements.label: C
statements.text: Measured during an end-expiratory hold manoeuvre

statements.label: D
statements.text: Normally 5-10 cmH2O

questions.question: A patient on sodium nitroprusside infusion requires monitoring for cyanide toxicity. Which of the following does NOT increase the risk of cyanide toxicity from sodium nitroprusside?
questions.explanation: 100% oxygen is the TREATMENT for cyanide toxicity — not a risk factor. It is administered alongside sodium thiosulphate (and optionally sodium nitrite or hydroxycobalamin) when cyanide toxicity is suspected. All other options increase risk: hepatic impairment reduces rhodanase-mediated cyanide detoxification; renal impairment impairs thiocyanate excretion leading to accumulation; prolonged high-dose infusion (>3 mcg/kg/min for >72h) overwhelms the detoxification pathway; and the maximum rate of 10 mcg/kg/min should NOT be maintained for more than 10 minutes. Monitoring for cyanide toxicity (lactic acidosis, confusion, haemodynamic deterioration) is mandatory in high-risk patients.
options: Renal insufficiency (impaired thiocyanate excretion leading to accumulation)
Co-administration of 100% oxygen
Infusion rates exceeding 3 mcg/kg/min for more than 72 hours
Hepatic insufficiency (impaired rhodanase activity reducing cyanide-to-thiocyanate conversion)
Running the maximum infusion rate of 10 mcg/kg/min for extended periods

questions.question: A 19-year-old man with sickle cell disease is admitted to hospital with pleuritic chest pain. He has a respiratory rate of 26 breaths/min and SpO2 92% on air. Which of the following would be suggestive of an acute chest crisis?
questions.explanation: Acute chest syndrome (ACS) should be suspected in any patient with sickle cell disease and acute respiratory symptoms. Radiological changes can be absent during the initial phase but often develop in the following days; segmental, lobar or multi-lobar consolidation is typical, whereas bilateral infiltrates can occur in ARDS or fluid overload, which can mimic rather than confirm ACS. Fever, chest pain, dyspnoea and hypoxia are all common features of ACS, and pneumonia - including atypical organisms such as Mycoplasma - is a common precipitant. Wheeze can occasionally be present in children with ACS but is a rare finding in adults.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Positive Mycoplasma serology

statements.label: B
statements.text: Wheeze

statements.label: C
statements.text: Bilateral infiltrates on chest x-ray

statements.label: D
statements.text: Pyrexia >38.5C

questions.question: A haemodynamically stable, cooperative patient with COVID-19-related ARDS is hypoxaemic. Which non-invasive strategy is best supported for reducing the need for invasive ventilation?
questions.explanation: In COVID-19-related ARDS, both CPAP and high-flow nasal oxygen have been shown to reduce the need for invasive ventilation, distinguishing this population from ARDS of other causes. B misattributes the benefit to BIPAP alone, C forgoes a supported non-invasive trial, D imposes an unnecessary sequence, and E omits the oxygen-delivery component central to the evidence.
options: BIPAP, whereas CPAP and high-flow oxygen have not been shown to help here
Awake prone positioning without any oxygen-delivery device
High-flow nasal oxygen, but only after a trial of CPAP has failed
Early intubation in preference to any non-invasive support
Either CPAP or high-flow nasal oxygen

questions.question: A patient is on CVVHDF. To reliably achieve the KDIGO-recommended delivered effluent dose of 20-25 mL/kg/h, what is typically prescribed?
questions.explanation: Because interruptions and downtime reduce delivery, prescribing 30-35 mL/kg/h is usually needed to actually deliver 20-25 mL/kg/h. Prescribing exactly 20-25 tends to under-deliver, and doses above 35 add harm without outcome benefit.
options: 20-25 mL/kg/h
10-15 mL/kg/h
As high as the machine allows
Greater than 40 mL/kg/h
30-35 mL/kg/h

questions.question: Regarding evidence on the timing of tracheostomy:
questions.explanation: A 2015 Cochrane review finding lower mortality and a higher probability of ICU discharge by day 28 with early tracheostomy, a 2024 meta-analysis of 21 RCTs finding early tracheostomy (within 10 days) shortened ventilation duration and ICU stay versus late, and a 2023 review in non-neurologically injured patients finding no clear mortality benefit and likely being underpowered, are all accurately described. The claim that the 2024 meta-analysis also found early tracheostomy significantly reduced mortality and pneumonia is false — despite shortening ventilation and ICU stay, the 2024 meta-analysis did not show a significant reduction in mortality or pneumonia; the evidence on mortality remains genuinely conflicting.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A 2024 meta-analysis of 21 RCTs found early tracheostomy (within 10 days) shortened ventilation duration and ICU stay versus late.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A 2023 review in non-neurologically injured patients found no clear mortality benefit and was likely underpowered.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A 2015 Cochrane review found lower mortality and a higher probability of ICU discharge by day 28 with early tracheostomy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The 2024 meta-analysis also found early tracheostomy significantly reduced mortality and pneumonia.

questions.question: A 44-year-old with cancer cachexia has been fasting for 12 days after intestinal obstruction and weight loss of 15% over 2 months. Nutritional support is being planned. Regarding refeeding syndrome in ICU patients, which statement is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Refeeding syndrome occurs in approximately 30% of ICU patients — a much higher prevalence than commonly appreciated. The cardinal feature is hypophosphataemia, defined as serum phosphate falling below 0.65 mmol/L (some references use 0.71 mmol/L) within 72 hours of initiating nutritional support. The mechanism is intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium — driven by insulin release in response to exogenous glucose — into cells whose intracellular stores are depleted after prolonged starvation. Hypophosphataemia (not hyperkalaemia) is the primary electrolyte abnormality. Normal saline preloading has no proven role in prevention.
options: Refeeding syndrome can be prevented by normal saline preloading before commencing nutrition in at-risk patients
Refeeding syndrome affects only patients who have been completely fasting for more than 3 weeks

Refeeding syndrome is uncommon (<5%) in critically ill patients, because metabolic adaptation to starvation conserves intracellular electrolytes and prevents the shifts seen in outpatient malnutrition
Refeeding syndrome affects ~30% of critically ill patients and is characterised by hypophosphataemia (<0.65 mmol/L) developing within 72 hours of feeding initiation
The cardinal electrolyte abnormality of refeeding syndrome is hyperkalaemia, resulting from insulin-driven intracellular potassium release

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency room by ambulance after a car crash. On admission, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is 6. The patient is intubated and you order a CT. You receive the following image from the CT. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A subdural haematoma may appear crescent-shaped and can cross cranial sutures, because it lies below the dura; however, it will not cross the midline, as it is bound by the falx. It may extend along the falx or tentorium.
options: Traumatic axonal injury
Traumatic contusion
Subdural haematoma
Spontaneous SAH
Epidural haematoma

questions.question: Regarding fluid selection in septic shock resuscitation:
questions.explanation: Hydroxyethyl starch (HES) solutions are associated with higher mortality and a greater need for renal replacement therapy compared with crystalloids, and are strongly recommended against by the SSC — a strong recommendation backed by high-quality evidence from trials including 6S and CHEST. When a colloid is considered in septic shock, albumin is the preferred choice, with a target serum albumin concentration of approximately 30 g/L. Gelatin solutions, by contrast, lack robust randomised trial evidence supporting their safety in sepsis, so they are not a well-established alternative to crystalloids — the SSC suggests against gelatins too, though with weaker evidence than for HES. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign does not specifically recommend balanced crystalloids over 0.9% saline for sepsis, even though avoiding hyperchloraemia is emphasised; this remains a weak or no-specific-recommendation area rather than a firm recommendation for balanced solutions.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign currently recommends balanced crystalloids (e.g., Ringer's lactate) over 0.9% saline as first-line fluid in sepsis.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Gelatin solutions have robust randomised trial evidence supporting their safety in sepsis and represent a well-established alternative to crystalloids.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Hydroxyethyl starch (HES) solutions are associated with higher mortality and greater need for renal replacement therapy versus crystalloids and are strongly recommended against by the SSC.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When a colloid is considered in septic shock, albumin is the preferred choice with a target serum albumin concentration of approximately 30 g/L.

questions.question: The same patient, now on regional citrate anticoagulation in CVVHD mode, has a post-filter ionized calcium of 0.45 mmol/l six hours after starting therapy (target range approximately 0.2-0.35 mmol/l). What should you do?
questions.explanation: A post-filter ionized calcium above the target range indicates under-anticoagulation of the circuit, so the citrate-to-blood-flow ratio should be increased, according to the unit's protocol, to bring the post-filter calcium down into the target range. Lowering the ratio would worsen circuit anticoagulation further, leaving the value unchanged would not correct an out-of-range result, and switching to heparin or stopping anticoagulation altogether are not the appropriate response to a single monitoring value that can be corrected by adjusting the citrate dose.
options: Lower the citrate-to-blood-flow ratio
Increase the citrate-to-blood-flow ratio
Switch immediately to systemic heparin anticoagulation
Stop regional citrate anticoagulation and run the circuit without anticoagulation
Make no changes, since the value is close enough to target

questions.question: A family asks about the prognosis of a 76-year-old COPD patient who has been mechanically ventilated for acute exacerbation. What is the most accurate characterisation of long-term outcomes in mechanically ventilated COPD?
questions.explanation: The long-term prognosis for mechanically ventilated COPD patients is poor. Published studies report 6-month mortality ranging from 40–70% depending on patient selection, pre-exacerbation functional status, and comorbidities. Two-year mortality rates may approach 80%, and 5-year mortality may reach approximately 90%. Factors predicting poor outcome include dyspnoea at rest with hypoxaemia and hypercapnia, pulmonary hypertension, irreversible airflow obstruction, poor nutritional status, multiple prior exacerbations, and comorbid organ disease. These sobering statistics underscore the importance of advance care planning before mechanical ventilation, including discussion of patient preferences for intubation and ventilatory support with both patients and families while they retain decision-making capacity.
questions.section: Part V: Supportive Therapies and Complications
options: Mechanically ventilated COPD patients have a 6-month mortality rate of less than 10%, similar to ventilated community-acquired pneumonia
Two-year mortality after ventilated AECOPD is less than 20% in patients without significant cardiac comorbidities
The 5-year mortality rate for ventilated COPD is approximately 30–40%, similar to outcomes after mechanical ventilation for acute asthma
Six-month mortality for mechanically ventilated COPD ranges between 40–70% across studies, and 5-year mortality may approach 90%
Following a single MV episode for AECOPD, the majority of patients return to their pre-exacerbation functional baseline within 6 months, with excellent long-term prognosis

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman presents with cardiogenic shock, a troponin of 8000 ng/L, unobstructed coronary arteries on angiography, an ejection fraction of 15 per cent and new complete atrioventricular block. Which management step is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Fulminant myocarditis with shock and conduction disease warrants early consideration of temporary mechanical circulatory support, since many patients recover ventricular function completely if they survive the acute phase, and biopsy is indicated because giant cell and eosinophilic myocarditis are treatable with immunosuppression while lymphocytic disease generally is not. Starting immunosuppression blind is the plausible wrong answer that forfeits the diagnostic information. Full-dose beta-blockade in overt cardiogenic shock and non-steroidal drugs are both harmful in this setting.
options: Start high-dose non-steroidal anti-inflammatory therapy for the myocardial inflammation
Start immunosuppression empirically before establishing any histological diagnosis
Manage as an acute coronary syndrome with dual antiplatelet therapy and heparin
Start beta-blockade at full dose immediately to protect the heart
Consider temporary mechanical circulatory support and endomyocardial biopsy

questions.question: A 47-year-old man presents with acute shortness of breath and stridor, saturations of 68% on air, and chest x-ray findings of a left lower lobe pneumonia. His history includes ongoing radiotherapy for a glottic tumour. What is the most appropriate approach to facilitate invasive ventilation?
questions.explanation: In a patient with a friable glottic tumour and airway obstruction, fibreoptic intubation risks bleeding and a 'cork-in-the-bottle' effect as the scope passes through a narrowed airway, and neuromuscular blockade should not be avoided since it provides the best conditions to ventilate, intubate, and access the front of the neck if needed. The RAMP position is most useful in obesity rather than airway obstruction. Provided the patient is stable enough to transfer, induction in the operating theatre with an ENT surgeon available (for nasendoscopy, intubation, or emergency tracheostomy) offers the safest, best-resourced approach rather than immediate RSI in the emergency department.
options: Immediate rapid sequence induction in the emergency department
Use of the RAMP position
Avoidance of neuromuscular blockade
Induction of anaesthesia in the operating theatre with an ENT surgeon available
Awake fibreoptic intubation

questions.question: A 59-year-old man with suspected sepsis has MAP 61 mmHg. Before administering a fluid bolus, the registrar performs a passive leg raise (PLR) and observes a 14% increase in cardiac output. What is the key clinical advantage of PLR over a traditional 500 mL crystalloid bolus for assessing fluid responsiveness?
questions.explanation: The passive leg raise mobilises venous blood from the lower limb and splanchnic reservoir into the central circulation, providing a reversible preload challenge. If cardiac output rises, the patient is preload-responsive and a fluid bolus is likely to be beneficial. Critically, the effect is completely reversed when the legs are lowered — no net fluid is administered, unlike a traditional bolus. Believing PLR can be performed and interpreted accurately without any haemodynamic monitoring device is a near-miss: accurate CO measurement (arterial waveform analysis, Doppler) is required to detect the response; PLR cannot be reliably interpreted by clinical examination alone. PLR does not avoid a hypotension risk that doesn't routinely accompany careful crystalloid boluses in the first place, it is not inherently more precise than pulse-pressure monitoring during a bolus, and its main advantage is reversibility rather than simply being faster to perform.
options: PLR is a reversible autotransfusion that tests preload responsiveness without giving IV fluid — fully reversible on lowering the legs
PLR provides a more precise quantification of cardiac output change than monitoring arterial pulse pressure during a fluid bolus.
PLR is faster to perform than a fluid challenge and therefore reduces time to initiation of vasopressors.
PLR can be performed and interpreted accurately without any haemodynamic monitoring device.
PLR avoids the risk of precipitous hypotension that routinely accompanies rapid crystalloid boluses in septic shock.

questions.question: A 21-year-old male is brought to the accident and emergency department after driving off the road. He is spontaneously breathing with 10 L/min of oxygen on a facemask. At admission his blood pressure is 95/45mmHg, heart rate 115/min, SpO2 92%, with a deep and regular respiratory rate of 35/min and GCS is 7. What type of cause of coma is most likely?
questions.explanation: The evaluation of the respiratory pattern may provide clues to the cause of the coma and to the localisation of the brain pathology (Validation of a new coma scale: the FOUR score, Wijdicks et al, Ann Neurol 2015). This deep, regular (Kussmaul-type) breathing pattern suggests a metabolic origin of coma, such as diabetic ketoacidosis or other severe causes of metabolic acidosis.
options: Increased intracranial pressure
Infection
An immune-mediated cause such as an acute demyelinating encephalomyelitis
Metabolic origin
Neoplastic

questions.question: In addition to end-expiratory flow persistence, the Paw waveform in a patient with severe COPD on volume-controlled ventilation changes shape from linear to convex at end-inspiration. What does the convex Paw shape indicate?
questions.explanation: During volume-controlled ventilation at constant tidal volume, the Paw waveform is normally linear (reflecting constant resistance and compliance). A convex shape at end-inspiration indicates that compliance is progressively decreasing as the breath proceeds. This occurs when dynamic hyperinflation has advanced to the point where the lung at end-inspiration approaches TLC — the region of lowest compliance on the pressure-volume curve. As compliance falls in this region, more pressure is required per unit of additional volume, producing a convex waveform. This sign, combined with end-expiratory flow persistence, identifies severe hyperinflation and should prompt urgent reduction of minute ventilation.
questions.section: Part IV: Ventilatory Support and Mechanics
options: Auto-triggering from a small undetected circuit leak adds a secondary flow pulse at end-inspiration, which creates a pressure overshoot artefact that mimics the convex waveform of reduced compliance
The respiratory system approaches TLC at end-inspiration, where compliance is reduced, reflecting severe dynamic hyperinflation
The convex shape reflects ETT obstruction increasing resistance during the final portion of each inspiration
The inspiratory pause time is too short, causing incomplete pressure oscillations in the ventilator circuit at the end of inflation that appear as a convex upward deflection in the pressure tracing
Decreased chest wall compliance from abdominal compartment syndrome or obesity-hypoventilation

questions.question: Which of the following suggest a condition of severely decreased ventilatory muscle function:
questions.explanation: Peak expiratory flow is not a test of muscle strength, so it does not indicate ventilatory muscle function; it mainly reflects large-airway calibre. A postural fall in FVC on lying supine, an absolute FVC below 1 L, and a substantial (>50%) decline from baseline are all recognised markers of severely compromised ventilatory muscle function.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A decline in Forced Vital Capacity of more than 50% from baseline value.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An Forced Vital Capacity of less than 1 L

statements.label: C
statements.text: A peak expiratory flow rate of less than 20%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A fall in Forced Vital Capacity when assuming the supine position from the seated or standing one

questions.question: Which of the following statements about different antibiotic (classes) are true?
questions.explanation: Betalactams display time-dependent killing characteristics — effective killing is determined by the time the free drug concentration remains above the MIC (A correct). Studies show ciprofloxacin is often dosed too low in the severely ill; three-times-daily dosing is recommended to optimise the AUC/MIC ratio in this population (B correct). There is only a very small chance of cross-reactivity between penicillin and most cephalosporins, particularly third-generation agents, making this a generally safe alternative even with type 1 penicillin allergy (C correct). Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) of vancomycin both helps avoid toxicity and improves therapeutic effectiveness — making monitoring mandatory in practice (D correct). References: Roger C et al. J Antimicrob Chemother. 2016 Jun;71(6):1643-50; Lteif L, Eiland LS. Pharmacy (Basel). 2019 Jul 17;7(3).

statements.label: A
statements.text: Monitoring drug levels in vancomycin therapy is mandatory

statements.label: B
statements.text: In case of type 1 penicillin allergy choosing a third generation cephalosporin as an alternative is a safe option

statements.label: C
statements.text: Ciprofloxacin should be dosed three times daily in the severely ill

statements.label: D
statements.text: Effective killing by betalactams is determined by the time above MIC

questions.question: What has recent evidence shown about alternating NIV with HFNC (versus HFNC alone) after extubation in high-risk patients?
questions.explanation: Alternating NIV with HFNC, compared with high-flow nasal oxygen alone, significantly decreases reintubation in patients at high risk of extubation failure, potentially combining benefits of both modalities.
questions.section: The role of NIV and HFNC in weaning failure
options: It significantly increases reintubation compared with HFNC alone
This combined strategy has never been studied in a clinical trial
HFNC alone is always contraindicated in high-risk patients after extubation
There is no difference between the strategies in any measured outcome
It significantly decreases reintubation versus high-flow nasal oxygen alone

questions.question: A patient with an acute anterior STEMI develops the annotated rhythm strip shown, confirming second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II, with a wide QRS complex. Based on the PACT module's guidance, what is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Mobitz type II block with a wide QRS complex, especially in the context of anterior myocardial infarction, is a specific indication for temporary backup pacing. In anterior MI, AV block usually reflects infranodal (bundle) disease and can progress abruptly and without warning to complete heart block with a slow, unreliable escape rhythm — a combination associated with severe left ventricular dysfunction and high mortality. Unlike inferior MI (where block is usually nodal, transient, and often atropine-responsive), anterior MI block is not reliably improved by atropine, since atropine acts on the sinus and AV node rather than infranodal tissue — reaching for antiarrhythmics or simply waiting for hypotension would both dangerously delay pacing in a high-risk situation.
options: Administer atropine 0.5 mg IV as the definitive treatment, since it reliably improves infranodal block
No action is needed unless the patient becomes hypotensive, since anterior MI block is typically transient and resolves spontaneously within hours
Arrange temporary backup pacing; this combination carries a significant risk of abrupt progression to complete heart block
Continue observation only; Mobitz type II carries the same low risk of progression as Mobitz type I
Treat with an antiarrhythmic drug to stabilise the conduction system

questions.question: Immediately after extubation of a patient at high risk for laryngeal oedema, you hear inspiratory stridor. A few minutes later, SpO2 is 85% on FiO2 1.0 with a respiratory rate of 40/min. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.explanation: [UNCONFIRMED] Reformulated from SBA scenario. With hypoxaemia and marked tachypnoea, the priority is securing the airway by re-intubating and stabilising on sedation and ventilation; nasoendoscopy to confirm laryngeal oedema and parenteral steroids follow once the diagnosis is confirmed and the patient is stable. Nebulised adrenaline, HFNO, or steroids alone do not address this degree of acute compromise.
options: Re-intubate, then sedate and ventilate until stability is achieved, before confirming the diagnosis endoscopically
Start high-flow nasal oxygen and reassess in 30 minutes
Reassure the patient and encourage deep breathing, as stridor typically resolves spontaneously
Give intravenous corticosteroids and await response before considering intubation
Give nebulised adrenaline and observe on the ward

questions.question: Regarding energy targets in the acute and later phases of critical illness:
questions.explanation: Full caloric targets from day 1 are not recommended; approximately 20 kcal/kg/day in the acute phase is generally accepted, with full doses after day 7. Actual body weight systematically overestimates energy needs in obese patients — ideal body weight is recommended. Pyrexia and agitation do genuinely increase energy expenditure and justify upward adjustment, while hypothermia and deep sedation reduce it. The recommendation to initiate supplemental PN after day 7 if enteral nutrition remains insufficient is consistent with current guidelines.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Pyrexia, agitation, and active rehabilitation increase energy expenditure and may justify upward adjustment of nutritional targets

statements.label: B
statements.text: In obese patients (BMI >30 kg/m²), actual body weight should always be used to calculate energy targets using predictive equations, as metabolic demands are proportional to actual weight

statements.label: C
statements.text: After day 7 in the ICU, if the patient cannot receive full caloric intake enterally, supplemental or total parenteral nutrition should be considered to meet nutritional targets

statements.label: D
statements.text: Full caloric targets of 25 kcal/kg/day should be delivered from day 1 of ICU admission in all mechanically ventilated patients to prevent cumulative energy deficit

questions.question: A 34-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV (no prior cART) is admitted to ICU with a 3-week history of progressive dyspnoea and non-productive cough. CD4 count is 145 cells/µL. PaO2 on room air is 62 mmHg. High-resolution CT shows bilateral perihilar ground-glass opacities sparing the periphery with intraparenchymal cysts. Which treatment regimen is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: This presentation is classic for PCP: subacute course over weeks, CD4 <200 cells/µL, perihilar bilateral ground-glass opacities with peripheral sparing and intraparenchymal cysts. TMP-SMX is the treatment of choice. Adjunctive prednisone is mandatory when PaO2 <70 mmHg on room air, reducing respiratory deterioration and mortality by attenuating the inflammatory response to dying fungi. Giving TMP-SMX alone without prednisone is the near-miss: the antimicrobial choice is correct but omits a step that is critically important at this level of hypoxaemia. CMV pneumonitis is much less likely with this subacute presentation and typical CT pattern.
questions.section: The ICU patient with HIV disease
options: TMP-SMX plus prednisone
TMP-SMX alone
IV liposomal amphotericin B
IV ganciclovir
IV ceftriaxone plus azithromycin

questions.question: A 67-year-old woman treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics for 8 days develops profuse watery diarrhoea (8 bowel motions per day), fever (38.3 degrees C), and leukocytosis (WBC 22,000/mm3). A C. difficile enzyme immunoassay (EIA) for toxin is ordered. Which of the following BEST describes the diagnostic performance of the EIA?
questions.explanation: The EIA for C. difficile toxin has a wide and variable sensitivity range of 29-86% — a negative result does not reliably exclude CDI in high-pretest-probability patients. Given this poor sensitivity, a negative EIA in a patient with profuse antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and leukocytosis should prompt further testing, such as a PCR-based assay, rather than being treated as sufficient on its own to exclude infection — the key trap here. Claiming sensitivity of approximately 95% and specificity above 98% vastly overstates the EIA's actual performance. EIA is performed on unformed or liquid stool, not formed stool, so restricting testing to formed samples is incorrect. EIA also cannot reliably distinguish between toxin A-only and toxin A/B producing strains.
questions.section: Laboratory Investigations, Microbiological Testing and Imaging
options: EIA should only be performed on formed stool samples to reduce false-positive rates
Sensitivity approximately 95% and specificity above 98%, making it highly reliable for ruling in and out CDI
Sensitivity ranges from 29-86% and performance is variable, meaning a negative result does not reliably exclude CDI
A negative EIA result in this clinical presentation is sufficient to exclude C. difficile infection
EIA can reliably distinguish between toxin A-only and toxin A/B producing strains

questions.question: You are called to assist with a 70-year-old woman who underwent an urgent surgical tracheostomy 2 days previously for airway obstruction due to laryngeal cancer, following a failed intubation by an experienced anaesthetist. She now has a respiratory rate of 35, a see-saw respiratory pattern, and saturations of 86% on FiO2 0.5. What is the safest management option?
questions.explanation: A systematic algorithmic approach to tracheostomy emergencies both improves the situation and helps diagnose the problem simultaneously. Removing the tracheostomy could be fatal, since this patient (known failed intubation, laryngeal cancer) is likely to be very difficult to re-intubate, and re-inserting a tube into a tracheostomy only 2 days old is dangerous in inexperienced hands. Checking tube position via bronchoscopy is reasonable but slow and needs higher-level skill without providing an immediate remedy, and simply increasing FiO2 may improve saturations without treating the underlying obstruction.
options: Increase the FiO2 to 1.0 and ask for an arterial blood gas
Call for senior help. Provide oxygen by face mask and via the tracheostomy tube. Attach capnography. Assess the patency of the tracheostomy using a suction catheter and re-assess
Request a bronchoscope and assess the position of the tracheostomy tube
Remove the tracheostomy tube and re-intubate the patient in a standard fashion
Deflate the tracheostomy tube cuff and reposition the tracheostomy tube

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman was admitted to intensive care following an overdose and has now been ventilated for 17 days. She failed an attempt at extubation 10 days into her stay. The following factors predict an increased chance of unsuccessful extubation:
questions.explanation: [UNCONFIRMED] Risk factors for failure to extubate include age older than 65, medical reason for admission, pre-existing cardiorespiratory disease, longer ventilation duration, higher illness severity, anaemia, previous unplanned extubations, impaired neurological status, weak cough with high secretion load, and positive (not negative) fluid balance. The negative-fluid-balance statement is corrected from the source screenshot: the on-screen marker scored 'True' as correct, but this directly contradicts the ESICM feedback text, which names positive fluid balance as the risk factor — the same type of marker/feedback mismatch seen previously in aw1_fk03. Corrected here to False in line with the written feedback.

statements.label: A
statements.text: New diagnosis of ventilator-associated pneumonia with a productive chest

statements.label: B
statements.text: Previous good health

statements.label: C
statements.text: Age 45 years

statements.label: D
statements.text: Negative fluid balance for the length of stay

questions.question:
A 46-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity (BMI 38), ischaemic heart disease, a pre-operative haemoglobin of 105 g/L and CKD stage 2, is admitted still intubated and ventilated to the general ICU after a difficult anterior resection for a rectal carcinoma. He required 3 units of blood during surgery and is admitted to the unit on 0.4 µg/kg/min of noradrenaline. His capillary refill time is > 3 seconds and he is cold with a temperature of 35.2 °C. His blood pressure is 110/55 mmHg, heart rate is a regular 126 beats per minute. His arterial blood gas reveals adequate oxygenation on FiO2 of 0.4, a pH 7.27, PaCO2 4.3 kPa (32 mmHg), blood glucose of 14.9 mmol/L, base excess of -6.8 and lactate of 4.1 mmol/L. His urine output is 15 mL/h and haemoglobin is 71 g/L.

The modifiable risk factors in the ICU for developing an AKI include:
questions.explanation: This patient has several risk factors for developing AKI. His past medical history (type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity, ischaemic heart disease, CKD, anaemia) are all associated with increased AKI risk. Prior to surgery anaemia could be corrected but the remainder would be difficult to modify in a timely fashion prior to urgent surgery. On admission to ICU there is evidence of worsening anaemia, hypovolaemia, and hyperglycaemia. All of these could have been avoided during surgery and can be managed on ICU and therefore are modifiable risks. The other listed combinations each include non-modifiable factors such as diabetes, malignancy, and ischaemic heart disease.
options: Hypovolaemia, anaemia, hyperglycaemia
Malignancy, ischaemic heart disease, obesity
Hyperglycaemia, anaemia, malignancy, obesity
Type 2 diabetes mellitus, anaemia, malignancy, hypovolaemia, CKD stage 2

questions.question: Augmented renal clearance in the critically ill is conventionally defined as a measured creatinine clearance exceeding:
questions.explanation: Augmented renal clearance is defined as a creatinine clearance greater than 130 mL/min/1.73 m2. Lower values fall within the normal range, and higher cut-offs would miss many affected patients who are already underdosed.
options: 90 mL/min/1.73 m2

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the diagnosis of atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome is NOT correct?
questions.explanation: Between 30 and 40% of patients with atypical HUS have neither a detectable complement gene mutation nor autoantibodies, so a negative genetic workup cannot exclude the diagnosis and must not delay treatment; genetic testing is more useful for prognosis, treatment duration and family counselling. The diagnosis rests on excluding TTP and Shiga toxin-related HUS while treating empirically within 24 hours when suspicion is high. Prodromal diarrhoea occurs in up to 28% of cases, so its presence is a classic trap rather than a discriminator, and complement protein levels take too long to guide the acute decision.
questions.section: Atypical haemolytic uremic syndrome: Diagnostic workup and differential diagnoses
options: A history of prodromal diarrhoea does not exclude the diagnosis
Complement protein levels are more useful for later confirmation than for acute decisions
It remains a diagnosis of exclusion requiring systematic exclusion of TTP and Shiga toxin-associated HUS
The absence of a detectable complement gene mutation excludes the diagnosis
Treatment should be started within 24 hours where suspicion is high, before confirmatory results return

questions.question: A nutrition support team member recommends an immune-modulating enteral formula containing glutamine, arginine, omega-3 fatty acids, and selenium for a 55-year-old trauma patient. What is the most appropriate response?
questions.explanation: Immunonutrients — including glutamine, arginine, omega-3 fatty acids, and pharmacological doses of selenium, vitamin C, E, beta-carotene, and zinc — have theoretical immune-modulating properties. Despite positive results in early pilot studies, large RCTs in critically ill patients have not confirmed benefit, and some found harm (particularly high-dose glutamine in multiple organ failure). Routine administration of these immunonutrients is not recommended in current ESPEN guidelines for unselected critically ill patients, including trauma patients.
options: Only selenium and vitamin C from this list have proven benefit; arginine and omega-3 fatty acids should be excluded
Immune-modulating formulas are only contraindicated in haematological malignancy and can be used freely in trauma

Routine use of immunonutrients is not recommended; large RCTs have not confirmed benefit in critically ill patients and some have shown harm, including potential mortality harm with high-dose glutamine in MOF
These nutrients have shown consistent mortality benefit across large RCTs and should be used routinely

Immune-modulating formulas containing glutamine, arginine, omega-3, and selenium are strongly recommended by ESPEN for trauma patients given their consistent mortality benefit across multiple large randomised controlled trials

questions.question: Regarding special clinical contexts for bradyarrhythmia:
questions.explanation: The aortic-root-abscess association with new conduction disease in endocarditis, the frequent resolution of Lyme-associated AV block with antibiotics, and the temporary-pacemaker bridge strategy after TAVR are all correct. Epicardial pacing wires are placed directly on the heart's epicardial surface during the surgical procedure itself, not inserted percutaneously via the femoral vein afterward — that describes a different, transvenous technique used in other clinical scenarios, so this statement is false.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Epicardial temporary pacing wires placed during cardiac surgery are typically inserted percutaneously via the femoral vein after the operation is complete.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Patients who develop conduction abnormalities after TAVR are managed with a temporary pacemaker while being evaluated for a permanent device.

statements.label: C
statements.text: New AV block or bundle branch block in a patient with aortic valve infective endocarditis implies an aortic root abscess.

statements.label: D
statements.text: AV block associated with Lyme disease myocarditis frequently resolves with antibiotic treatment.

questions.question: What is the recommended cuff pressure of a cuffed tracheostomy or endotracheal tube?
questions.explanation: The cuff of an endotracheal or tracheostomy tube must seal against the tracheal mucosa to permit positive pressure ventilation without an air leak, and must be regularly monitored with a manometer. Low cuff pressures (below 20 cmH2O) are associated with ineffective ventilation, aspiration, and ventilator-associated pneumonia, while pressures above 30 cmH2O risk tracheal mucosal necrosis and stenosis — a target range of 20-30 cmH2O balances these risks.
options: 0 to 10 cmH2O
30 to 40 cmH2O
20 to 30 cmH2O
40 to 50 cmH2O
10 to 20 cmH2O

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Le Fort fractures and maxillofacial trauma are correct?
questions.explanation: Le Fort III (not Le Fort II) causes craniofacial separation involving the zygomatic arches. Le Fort II is pyramidal and extends through the orbits and nasal bones but spares the zygomatic arches. All Le Fort levels mandate anticipation of a difficult airway due to altered anatomy, bleeding, and swelling. Le Fort I is the horizontal maxillary fracture. Pulsatile exophthalmos indicates a carotid–cavernous fistula and is a serious vascular complication requiring urgent evaluation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Le Fort I produces palate-facial separation through a horizontal fracture at the level of the lower maxilla.

statements.label: B
statements.text: All Le Fort fracture levels require anticipation of a difficult airway, and a competent airway provider should be immediately available.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Le Fort II fractures cause craniofacial separation by extending through the zygomatic arches and fully detaching the midface from the skull base.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Pulsatile exophthalmos following facial trauma is a benign finding caused by periorbital oedema.

questions.question: Regarding ethics in clinical research involving ICU patients:
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Helsinki (1964, revised multiple times) is the primary international framework for research ethics in humans. Research on ICU patients is ethically justifiable when appropriately regulated — it requires robust safeguards including ethics committee oversight, proxy or deferred consent, and independent safety monitoring. Deferred consent (enrolling first, seeking retroactive consent) is a recognised approach for emergency research, supported by evidence of patient and proxy acceptance. The Nuremberg Code addressed explicit non-consensual Nazi experimentation — it does not prohibit deferred consent in contemporary regulated research.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Patients' inability to provide informed consent means research on the ICU population is ethically unjustifiable and must not be conducted

statements.label: B
statements.text: Deferred consent — enrolling patients before consent and seeking retroactive consent — is prohibited under the Nuremberg Code

statements.label: C
statements.text: Proxy consent from a legal surrogate or family member is an accepted and frequently used alternative to patient consent in ICU research

statements.label: D
statements.text: The Declaration of Helsinki provides internationally recognised ethical guidelines for research in humans and has been revised multiple times since its adoption in 1964

questions.question: Using the Sedation–Agitation Scale (SAS), a mechanically ventilated patient requires both loud verbal commands AND a sternal rub before opening eyes and following a simple command. What is the SAS score?
questions.explanation: SAS 3 (Sedated) describes a patient who will awaken and follow commands but requires loud verbal or physical stimuli to do so. SAS 2 (Very sedated) arouses to physical stimuli but does not awaken, communicate, or follow commands — only spontaneous movements are seen. SAS 1 (Unresponsive) shows minimal or no response to noxious stimuli. SAS 4 (Calm and cooperative) awakens easily to commands without physical stimulation. PAD guidelines recommend RASS and SAS as the two most validated and reliable agitation/sedation scales for ICU use.
options: SAS 3 — Sedated
SAS 4 — Calm and cooperative
SAS 5 — Agitated
SAS 1 — Unresponsive
SAS 2 — Very sedated

questions.question: The following is a true statement regarding the use of Ilofotase alfa in sepsis:
questions.explanation: Ilofotase alfa is exogenous recombinant alkaline phosphatase which was designed to detoxify PAMPs (e.g., endotoxin) and de-phosphorylates DAMPs (ATP — the dephosphorylating-ATP mechanism is indeed correct). Adenosine released after ATP dephosphorylation activates immunosuppressive pathways via A2 alpha receptors, reducing release of pro-inflammatory mediators including TNF-alpha (the TNF-alpha-metabolism description describes a secondary mechanism, not the primary action). However, none of the individual statements as written is fully correct: the dephosphorylating-ATP mechanism is actually correct on its own — but the question asks for the single TRUE statement among the options, and ESICM's answer is 'none of the above'. Ilofotase alfa is NOT the drug of choice for toxic shock syndrome or disseminated intravascular coagulation. In the STOP-AKI trial, it failed to show benefit on creatinine clearance but improved long-term renal function.
options: Mechanism of action by enhancing the metabolism of TNF alpha
Mechanism of action is by dephosphorylating ATP
None of the above is correct
It is the drug of choice for toxic shock syndrome caused by gram positive bacteria
It is the drug of choice for disseminated intravascular coagulation related to Sepsis

questions.question: Regarding patient outcomes after AKI:
questions.explanation: The short-term effects of AKI (acid-base disturbance, uraemia, fluid overload) occur acutely as part of the syndrome itself, independent of any progression to CKD. A definitive causal mechanism linking AKI to long-term adverse outcomes remains unproven and is actively debated, with proposed explanations including organ cross-talk and cytokine-mediated effects.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Long-term effects of AKI include increased hospital readmission within 90 days and increased likelihood of transfer to a long-term care facility.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Short-term effects of AKI, such as acid-base disturbance and uraemia, only become apparent after progression to chronic kidney disease.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A definitive causal mechanism linking AKI to adverse long-term outcomes has been firmly established and is no longer debated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Increasing severity of AKI is associated with increased mortality risk across diverse clinical settings, including cardiac surgery, trauma, and critical illness.

questions.question: A 64-year-old patient is admitted to the ICU with respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. Which of the following is NOT a recommended component of the clinical nutritional assessment in this patient?
questions.explanation: A comprehensive clinical nutritional assessment includes severity of illness, presence of comorbidities, days in hospital prior to ICU admission, predicted length of stay, admission diagnosis, type of ventilation, medications (particularly propofol for caloric contribution), CRRT status (for amino acid losses and citrate energy), and drain output (for protein losses). Serum albumin should NOT be used as the primary marker of protein depletion to guide nutritional decisions in critically ill patients — it reflects disease severity and fluid distribution, not acute nutritional status, and is no longer recommended for initial nutritional assessment in inpatients.
options: Predicted length of ICU stay and presence of co-morbid disease
Serum albumin as the primary indicator of protein depletion guiding the nutritional prescription
Severity of illness based on APACHE II and SOFA scores
Presence and duration of continuous renal replacement therapy
Review of medications including rate and formulation of any propofol infusion

questions.question: Regarding the comparative evidence for enteral versus parenteral nutrition in critically ill patients:
questions.explanation: PN is associated with more infectious complications than EN — not fewer — and is not the preferred route simply because central access is available. The CALORIES trial found no significant mortality difference between early EN and PN, not a PN benefit. EN's advantages include preservation of gut mucosal integrity via luminal stimulation and maintenance of GALT immunological function, which are well-established physiological advantages over PN. EN is also markedly cheaper than PN.

statements.label: A
statements.text: EN preserves gut mucosal integrity and maintains the function of gut-associated lymphoid tissue in ways that PN does not

statements.label: B
statements.text: The CALORIES trial demonstrated that early PN significantly reduces 30-day mortality compared with early EN in critically ill adults

statements.label: C
statements.text: EN is substantially less expensive to provide than PN for an equivalent caloric target in the ICU

statements.label: D
statements.text: PN is associated with fewer infectious complications than EN and should be the preferred route in all ICU patients when central access is already in place

questions.question: This CT brain is from a patient following a severe deceleration injury. The pattern of multiple bilateral hyperdense lesions is MOST consistent with which injury mechanism?
questions.explanation: Multiple bilateral hyperdense lesions represent haemorrhagic contusions at the impact site (coup) and the diametrically opposite surface (contrecoup) from the acceleration-deceleration mechanism. Frontal and temporal poles are classically affected. This pattern is distinct from diffuse axonal injury, which causes microscopic disruption not reliably visible on CT.
questions.section: TBI Part II: Secondary Brain Injury
options: Coup-contrecoup haemorrhagic brain contusions
Bilateral epidural haematomas from temporal fractures
Diffuse axonal injury from pure rotational forces
Acute subdural haematoma from bridging vein rupture
Post-traumatic vasospasm with bilateral infarction

questions.question: Alveolar units that repetitively collapse at end-expiration and reopen with each breath are subject to which injurious mechanism?
questions.explanation: Repetitive collapse and reopening generates high dynamic strain and shear stress - atelectrauma - distinct from volutrauma or barotrauma, though the mechanisms interrelate. The other options misattribute the injury or deny it.
options: A pattern with no described injurious mechanism
Atelectrauma, from high dynamic strain and shear stress as units recruit and derecruit
Oxygen toxicity, unrelated to mechanical forces
Barotrauma, caused solely by excessive absolute airway pressure
Volutrauma, caused solely by excessive tidal volume regardless of recruitment

questions.question: A 27-year-old male remains agitated and confused after an IV bolus of 50% glucose, and a head CT is requested to investigate his encephalopathy. How should he be prepared for the CT scan?
questions.explanation: An agitated, confused patient cannot be safely managed in the CT suite without a secured airway and full monitoring — intubation and ventilation prior to transfer, with an airway-trained doctor and resuscitation equipment present, is the safe approach. Sedation alone, restraint, or delaying the scan risk airway compromise or missing time-critical pathology.
options: Intubate and ventilate prior to transfer, with full monitoring accompanied by an airway-trained doctor and resuscitation equipment
Sedate with a single benzodiazepine dose without securing the airway
Physically restrain the patient and transfer without sedation
Delay the CT scan until the patient settles spontaneously
Perform the scan awake with light sedation and no additional monitoring

questions.question: A 31-year-old sustains 45% total body surface area burns and weighs 75 kg. Regarding his protein requirements, which statement is MOST accurate?
questions.explanation: The recommended protein ceiling of 2.0 g/kg/day does not apply when there are substantial ongoing protein losses — extensive burns, large GI or enterocutaneous fistulae, and major urinary protein losses are all exceptions. In major burns, protein requirements can substantially exceed 2.0 g/kg/day and must be individually calculated based on wound severity, extent of burns, and monitoring of nitrogen balance. Standard protein targets apply to the general ICU population; individualisation based on losses is essential in burns.
options: Standard protein targets of 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day are sufficient and should not be exceeded in burns patients
Protein requirements in burns are lower than other critical illness because impaired synthetic capacity limits protein utilisation
Branched-chain amino acids should replace standard balanced amino acid solutions in all major burns patients
Protein restriction below 1.0 g/kg/day protects renal function in burns patients with acute kidney injury
Protein intake may legitimately exceed 2.0 g/kg/day in patients with extensive burns given substantial ongoing protein losses

questions.question: Regarding antibiotic therapy during CRRT, which of the following statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Membrane type can influence antibiotic pharmacokinetics: polyacrylonitrile membranes have a high adsorbing capacity for certain antibiotics, such as aminoglycosides (up to around 25% of a dose), while polysulfone membranes adsorb virtually none, though this effect is limited mainly to the initial phase of treatment since adsorption saturates quickly. Higher protein binding reduces, rather than increases, removal by CRRT, since only the free fraction is available for extracorporeal exchange - for many antibiotics, CRRT actually increases clearance and doses need to be increased rather than reduced across the board. Because residual renal clearance is usually limited in AKI patients requiring RRT, antibiotic dosing should generally not be adjusted to residual creatinine clearance, and guidelines designed for chronic kidney disease patients do not account for the pharmacokinetic changes of critical illness, often leading to underdosing if applied here.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Antibiotic doses should always be adapted to patient's creatinine clearance (TDM)

statements.label: B
statements.text: Polyacrylonitrile membranes have a high adsorbing capacity for certain types of antibiotics

statements.label: C
statements.text: Doses of all antimicrobials should be reduced during CRRT

statements.label: D
statements.text: The higher the protein binding of a molecule, the higher its removal by CRRT.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about thrombocytopaenia is correct?
questions.explanation: For thrombocytopenic patients at high risk of haemorrhage without liver failure, citrate can be considered as anticoagulant management for intermittent and continuous renal dialysis. Intra-aortic balloon pump use does cause platelet consumption, ultrasound guidance does reduce CVC-related bleeding risk in thrombocytopenia, and neuraxial procedures are discouraged below a platelet count of 70-80x10^9/L, not 30-40x10^9/L.
options: Placement of a central venous catheter in a thrombocytopaenic patient is not associated with a reduced risk of bleeding if ultrasound guidance is used
Intra-aortic balloon pump use is not a cause of thrombocytopaenia
Thrombocytopaenia is associated with metronidazole
Neuraxial blockade in a thrombocytopaenic patient is not recommended if the platelet count is <30-40x10^9/L
Citrate can be considered for haemodialysis circuits in thrombocytopaenic patients

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman with known cirrhosis secondary to alcohol consumption is admitted with acute kidney injury. She has tense ascites and suffers from dyspnea. On admission: Serum Na+ 129 mmol/L, Creatinine 1.49 mg/dL (132 μmol/L) (2 days previously 0.9 mg/dL / 80 μmol/L), Urea 37.8 mg/dL. Paracentesis was performed (no spontaneous bacterial peritonitis), diuretics were discontinued and human albumin solution (HAS) was administered. The patient was hemodynamically stable (BP 100/65 mmHg) with no structural kidney abnormality on ultrasound. Two days later, serum creatinine remained elevated (1.57 mg/dL / 139 μmol/L). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: This is hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI): progressive renal impairment in cirrhosis with tense ascites, unresponsive to albumin/diuretic withdrawal, with a structurally normal kidney. HRS reflects splanchnic arterial vasodilation from portal hypertension causing effective arterial underfilling and compensatory renal vasoconstriction. Terlipressin plus albumin is the most effective evidence-based treatment; inotropes/vasopressors such as dobutamine, epinephrine, levosimendan or dopamine are not the specific therapy.
options: Dopamine
Levosimendan
Dobutamine
Terlipressin
Epinephrine

questions.question: Regarding causes of QRS complex widening on the ECG:
questions.explanation: Conducting system damage causing slow aberrant spread through ventricular myocardium and widening QRS is correct, as is pre-excitation via an accessory pathway bypassing the AV node and activating ventricular myocardium before the His-Purkinje system engages, producing the delta wave and widened QRS. Attributing QRS widening to first-degree AV block is false: it causes PR interval prolongation (delayed AV nodal conduction) but does NOT widen the QRS, since His-Purkinje activation is normal once the impulse passes the AV node. Ventricular pacing initiating activation from the pacing electrode in non-conducting myocardium and producing wide QRS is also correct — one of the five enumerated causes of QRS widening in the PACT module.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Bundle branch block (damage to the conducting system) is a recognised cause of QRS widening

statements.label: B
statements.text: Ventricular paced complexes produce broad, abnormal QRS morphology due to non-His-Purkinje ventricular activation

statements.label: C
statements.text: First-degree AV block causes QRS widening due to prolonged conduction through the His-Purkinje system

statements.label: D
statements.text: Conduction through an accessory AV pathway, as in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, causes QRS widening via pre-excitation

questions.question: Regarding the delivered dose of renal replacement therapy:
questions.explanation: Interruptions reduce, not increase, the delivered dose, temporary catheters give lower flows than fistulas, and critically ill ICU dialysis cannot match chronic outpatient delivery. The delivered dose is therefore often below what is prescribed.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Temporary catheters allow higher blood flows than fistulas

statements.label: B
statements.text: ICU intermittent dialysis delivers the same dose as chronic outpatient dialysis

statements.label: C
statements.text: The delivered dose is often lower than the prescribed dose

statements.label: D
statements.text: Interruptions for filter changes increase the delivered dose

questions.question: Assess each of the following statements concerning ESICM Acute Gastrointestinal Injury (AGI) grading.
questions.explanation: AGI Grade I represents self-limiting GI symptoms related to a known cause, expected in the post-operative period. AGI Grade II is GI dysfunction requiring therapeutic interventions (such as prokinetics for gastroparesis with GRV >500 mL) without systemic deterioration — not Grade III. AGI Grade III is sustained GI failure despite interventions, associated with persistent or worsening MODS. AGI Grade IV is life-threatening GI failure that directly drives ongoing haemodynamic instability and organ failure.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A ventilated patient with gastroparesis requiring prokinetics and GRV consistently above 500 mL, but without additional organ dysfunction, should be classified as AGI Grade III

statements.label: B
statements.text: Persistent GI paralysis despite erythromycin and postpyloric tube placement, associated with worsening acute kidney injury, should be classified as AGI Grade III

statements.label: C
statements.text: Bowel ischaemia with necrosis causing haemorrhagic shock and worsening multi-organ failure represents AGI Grade IV

statements.label: D
statements.text: Post-operative nausea and vomiting in an otherwise improving patient following uncomplicated elective bowel surgery represents AGI Grade I
